input.said: What does Seth use the Antikythera mechanism to show?

cases.reply:
He uses it as an early example that computers weren't always digital Turing machines. He says the earliest computers were analogue devices operating in continuous time, and the Antikythera mechanism, used for astronomical purposes, is his "excellent example." The point sits in his second argument, "Other Games In Town". There he argues that Turing-style computation is only one kind of computation, and that brains may depend on continuous, physical dynamics outside it [spya-gamzr3 spya-n393ru]. The article follows the mechanism with a second example, cybernetics-era analogue computers, and then neuromorphic and "mortal" computation [spya-zg9me8 spya-kjfjgm]. The article dates the mechanism to "around 2,000 BCE." That looks wrong. [Britannica](https://britannica.com/topic/Antikythera-mechanism) puts its manufacture at about 100 BCE, give or take 30 years. Other sources I found give dates from roughly 205 BCE to the 1st century BCE. The error doesn't affect Seth's point, which only needs the device to be an ancient analogue calculator.

input.said: What does Seth say about Chalmers' neural replacement thought experiment?

cases.reply:
Seth says the thought experiment fails because it assumes something impossible: a perfect silicon stand-in for a brain part. He says it "fails at its first hurdle" [spya-ahtr6e].

He first describes the experiment. It asks you to imagine swapping brain parts one by one for silicon equivalents that work exactly like the originals. The supposed conclusion is that consciousness must not depend on the material it runs on. He adds that it is often used to support the possibility of conscious AI, and that Hinton used it that way when claiming conscious AI already exists [spya-ahtr6e].

His objection rests on the brain's "deep multiscale integration," which he links to what philosophers call "generative entrenchment." Because of it, you can't assume a single neuron can be replaced by a silicon version with its input-output behaviour perfectly preserved [spya-jnwfxp]. His example is that some neurons fire spikes apparently to clear metabolic waste. A perfect silicon replacement would need its own silicon-based metabolism, which silicon isn't suited for [spya-un9fjn]. He concludes that the only seamless replacement for a biological neuron is another biological neuron, ideally the same one [spya-un9fjn].

My inference is that this belongs to his first argument, "brains are not computers." That argument holds that you can't cleanly separate what a brain does from what it is, which undercuts the idea that consciousness is a matter of computation [spya-zw2m7u spya-p4vmm0].

cases.reply:
He says McCulloch and Pitts showed in a landmark paper that networks of highly simplified abstract neurons can perform logical operations [spya-va8qxr]. 

The "Turing complete" result is a later step, and Seth credits it to Stephen Kleene and others. They showed that such networks, once given a tape-like memory as in a Turing machine, could in principle implement any algorithm [spya-va8qxr]. Figure 2's caption shows what one of these artificial neurons looks like. It is a unit that sums weighted inputs and passes the total through an activation function [spya-qknqjx].

In the argument, this sets up what he calls a "mathematical marriage of convenience." You can ignore the messy biology of real neurons and treat the brain as a network of simple summing units. His objection is that real brains have no sharp split between "mindware" and "wetware" [spya-b0086e].
